chunks: "Bulk capacitance is the large-value capacitance, typically tens to thousands of microfarads, that you put at the point where power enters a board or at a regulator's input or output.
It acts as a local energy tank for the slower and bigger part of the load's demands. It does a few things.
When a load suddenly asks for more current, the regulator takes a few microseconds to respond, so the bulk cap supplies the difference and limits the droop.
It smooths ripple on a converter input, since a buck draws pulsed current from its input. It provides hold-up, so a brief interruption of the source doesn't reset the system.
And at a connector it helps damp the inductance of the cable so a hot-plug doesn't ring. You size it by charge or energy.
For a 2 amp step where the regulator loop has a 100 kilohertz bandwidth and I can tolerate 100 millivolts, I need roughly change in I over (2 pi f c change in V) , about 32 microfarads.
What bulk capacitance doesn't do is fast transients. Big capacitors have high ESL, so above maybe a hundred kilohertz to a megahertz they look inductive.
That's why bulk sits alongside smaller ceramics, which cover the high-frequency end."
